case_info.scenario: A healthy 19-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type V presented with a 2-year history of bumps of the nose (Figure 1A). Physical examination was notable for several smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. The patient had previously been treated for moderate acne vulgaris of the face (temples, cheeks, nose, and chin), chest, and back that had since been well-controlled using tretinoin cream, 0.1%. The nasal papules persisted, despite resolution of the remainder of his acne without residual scarring. The patient was otherwise healthy without history of developmental delay, seizures, hypopigmented skin macules, or other notable cutaneous, cardiac, or neurologic lesions. A punch biopsy was obtained to guide further diagnosis and treatment.
case_info.caption: A, Smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. B, Superficial telangiectatic vessels, thick collagen bundles, and prominent sebaceous glands (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree with that assessment. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules are not a recognized standard diagnosis; the clinical description of firm, skin-colored papules on the nose in a young adult with Fitzpatrick skin type V is more characteristic of fibrous papules of the nose or early angiofibromas, which would be distinct from acne sequelae. 1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density).    - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.
